content:
A woman whose husband was killed in a cargo plane crash at Miami International Airport on Sunday has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Amazon, cargo airline 21 Air, the aircraft lessor and the two pilots who flew the plane.

Yaraisi Santiso Morejon filed the lawsuit in Miami-Dade County on Wednesday, alleging multiple acts of negligence led to the death of her 53-year-old husband, Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo. Rodriguez was one of five people killed when Amazon Air Flight 7598 veered off the runway and struck a passenger van carrying a cleaning crew who had just finished their last job before heading home.

Jorge Garcia, a lawyer at the Morgan & Morgan law firm representing Santiso, said: "This is a very hardworking family that came here from Cuba in 2011. They worked multiple jobs, really put down roots in the community, and are a very strong family."

Garcia said Rodriguez died instantly on impact. His survivors include his wife and their 22-year-old son, Ronaldo. The lawyer said Amazon had not reached out to the family, but the company told HuffPost it was trying to obtain contact information for the families of those affected by the crash.

The company also provided HuffPost with a statement issued Tuesday by spokesperson Kelly Nantel, which extended condolences to the families of the dead and said Amazon planned to cooperate fully with all relevant investigations.

Lawyer Mike Morgan said: "We believe it is important at this moment, based on the information available, given this avoidable tragedy, to immediately file this lawsuit to preserve the rights of Mr. Rodriguez's estate and to preserve any relevant evidence during the NTSB investigation."

The other four people killed were 55-year-old Rolando Aleman Leon, 75-year-old Julio C. Pineda, 53-year-old Carlos Acosta Fajardo, and 47-year-old Javierkys Reyes Quevedo. NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy described the scene as "absolute devastation," with the passenger van "torn to pieces."

The Boeing 767-300 crash sparked a massive fire and left five others seriously injured, including the two pilots, who have since been released from the hospital. Garcia and Morgan questioned the training and competence of Captain Joseph Carroll and First Officer Jaime Felipe Silva Molina when they spoke to reporters.

Morgan said: "From what we're hearing on the cockpit voice recorder, it was quite chaotic. We learned this morning that the throttles were still at full power 15 seconds before impact, which indicates the crew lacked a unified strategy and never declared an emergency, raising a lot of questions about what was going on in the cockpit at the time."

The NTSB opened its investigation into the crash this week, and investigators examined the aircraft on Tuesday. The lawyers said the aircraft operator, 21 Air, had previously received a series of safety complaints from senior employees, and alleged that Amazon knew or should have known about these safety deficiencies.

The lawsuit alleges: "This catastrophe was not an unavoidable accident, but a foreseeable and entirely preventable result of multiple concurrent acts of negligence." These include: "Pilot Carroll and Molina making human errors while attempting a high-speed landing in tailwind conditions and failing to execute the mandatory go-around procedure; systemic failures by defendants Amazon and 21 Air to ensure the pilots received adequate training, were physically fit and possessed proper aeronautical decision-making skills; and the use by the relevant defendants of a 32-year-old aircraft whose braking, thrust reverser and spoiler systems are under NTSB investigation."

The suit continues: "Any one of the aforementioned acts of negligence, standing alone, would have been sufficient to cause death. Several of them, taken together, caused catastrophic consequences."
